title: Forty Doors
logline: At a weekly lay meditation class, a teacher asks each newcomer about their life and then gives them a different, deliberately plain thing to attend to.

object.note: Object 10 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: A burden set down makes room for stillness: a town temple's lay meditation class, where each person is sent to their own plain object.

thread_out.thread: One plain object for each person becomes one stone held under one lamp for longer than seems reasonable, until its faults and its worth both show.

requirements: A real, regular lay meditation class with a willing teacher
Participants willing to be identified only as much as they choose
A room, not a forest retreat, to keep this distinct from Episode 1's monastery

suggestions.name: A town temple's lay meditation society
suggestions.why: Such weekly classes are common at temples across the island.
suggestions.verify: No specific temple or teacher is identified.

lesson.in_simple_terms: There is no single right way to settle the mind: a good teacher looks at who you are and gives you something that fits. And settling the mind is only a start; the texts say that seeing clearly is what frees.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: සිත සන්සුන් කිරීමට එකම නිවැරදි ක්‍රමයක් නැත; හොඳ ගුරුවරයෙක් එක් එක් කෙනාගේ ස්වභාවය බලා ඔවුන්ට ගැළපෙන කමටහනක් දෙයි, නමුත් සිත සන්සුන් වීම ආරම්භය පමණි.
lesson.the_teaching: The texts list forty meditation subjects (kammaṭṭhāna) for calm (samatha), from a plain clay disc (kasiṇa) to recalling the good qualities of others and one's own generosity, and say each should suit a person's temperament and be taken from a teacher. Each subject has its own reach: some can carry the mind into full absorption, others only close to it. The texts insist there are two kinds of work: calm, which quiets the hindrances, and insight (vipassanā), which sees things as changing, unsatisfying and not a self, and only insight brings the path. For lay people the Margaya describes a modest routine of half an hour to an hour a day.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: Several very different people arrive for the same weekly class, and in short, separate conversations the teacher asks about each person's life before suggesting what to attend to. When the room goes quiet, everyone is doing something different inside the same silence. What people say, or do not say, as they leave keeps the film honest that settling is a beginning, not an arrival.

key_terms.en: meditation subject; ground for the work of practice
insight meditation; seeing mind and matter as impermanent, suffering, non-self
a plain prepared object, such as a clay disc, used for calm meditation

lesson.caution: This is not 'focus on whatever you like' or mindfulness for stress relief: the texts match each subject to a person and a teacher, and place calm in the service of insight.
lesson.builds_on: The last film showed a burden set down; this one shows what the texts say can follow, a mind given room to settle, with each person starting from their own door.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
